title: AI-Generated Tests Still Need a Quality Gate
slack_text:
🧪 *QE Daily #005 — AI-Generated Tests Still Need a Quality Gate*

AI can accelerate test-design work, but generated scenarios are proposals — not evidence of coverage.

Common failure modes include fabricated requirements, duplicate scenarios, vague expected results, missing integration risks and tests that do not match the architecture.

*Hypothetical scenario*
An AI tool generates 60 test cases from a ticket. The list looks comprehensive, but the ticket never defined retry behaviour, several expected results are invented, and the highest-risk dependency is missing.

*Think like a QE*
Validate generated tests against approved sources. Separate confirmed requirements from assumptions. Deduplicate by risk/behaviour, then add missing technical and failure-path coverage.

*Challenge*
What quality gates would you require before accepting an AI-generated test plan?

*Takeaway*
AI can reduce drafting effort. Accountability for correctness and risk coverage still belongs to the engineer.

💬 Add one quality gate you would never skip.
thread_answer: Useful gates include source traceability, fact/assumption separation, requirement contradiction detection, duplicate detection, testability of expected results, architecture/dependency coverage, negative and failure-mode coverage, risk prioritisation, platform/locale/accessibility considerations where relevant, and explicit human approval before execution or publication.
linkedin_text:
QE Daily #005 — AI-generated tests still need a quality gate.

Generating 50 or 100 test cases in seconds feels productive. But volume is not the same as correctness or coverage.

AI-generated test plans can invent requirements, repeat the same behaviour under different wording, produce weak expected results, overlook dependencies, or assume an architecture that does not exist.

That means the valuable QE workflow is not simply ‘prompt → accept.’

It is closer to:

approved sources → generation → validation → risk review → human approval.

I want AI to remove drafting toil, surface possibilities and help structure analysis. I do not want it making unverified product decisions on my behalf.

The better we become at using AI, the more important our validation discipline becomes.

What quality gate would you require before accepting an AI-generated test plan?
